transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2026-04-15
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Carlos (Redwood SE), Dr. Emily Park (Horizon), Raj (Horizon), Sana (Horizon)

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for making time. Quick check in — weekly POC sync for Horizon Health, focusing on the quality evals and any regressions since we pushed the prompt tweaks last Friday. Carlos will run through the results, then we can talk guardrails and action items.

[00:18] Carlos: Cool, thanks Maya. Uh, quick note, I pulled together the evals into one sheet, there's a link in the notes. I ran the scoring across the baseline and the updated prompt set — we have two cohorts, clinical triage prompts and patient messaging prompts. Overall, accuracy metric is about flat, but we saw a few small regressions in triage severity assignment.

[00:40] Dr. Park: Right, we saw that too. A couple of prompts that used to mark 'urgent' are now 'high' which changes the downstream routing. That was a concern for the clinicians. It looks like one of the prompts where we added the phrasing to reduce hallucination impacted the severity heuristic.

[01:05] Raj: To add, the scoring rubric we used was the 0-3 clinical relevance scale from the doc you shared. There might be some rater variance, I think two of the raters interpreted the rubric slightly differently. We flagged inter-rater issues on about 8% of cases.

[01:30] Carlos: Noted. I also want to call out one oddity — in shorter context lengths the model tended to drop the qualifier 'immediate' when summarizing triage notes, which bumped severity down. That suggests prompt engineering plus maybe using a longer context window or pinning that phrase in the system prompt.

[01:55] Maya: Good, so sounds like a combination of prompt tweak regressions and annotation variance. For the prompt tweak regressions, can you identify the top 10 failing prompts by delta score?

[02:10] Carlos: Yes, I have that in the sheet. Top ones are: intake-12, intake-47, med-history-3, and a couple of patient-message templates. I'll export that as a separate tab.

[02:30] Sana: From a compliance angle, we also noticed two cases where the model included PHI verbatim in the suggested message text. It's only a couple, but our policy requires redaction or structured placeholders for any direct identifiers.

[02:52] Dr. Park: Can you say whether those PHI leaks were from hallucinated content or echoed back from the prompt? I know some prompts contain example names for training.

[03:08] Carlos: Looks like both. For one, the prompt included a patient example name, and the model echoed it. For another, the model made up a name when filling a suggested message. So we need guardrail rules to always replace detected identifiers with [REDACTED] or placeholders.

[03:30] Raj: We can add a post-processing redaction step on our side, but we prefer the model to avoid emitting PHI at all. Do you have a recommended pattern?

[03:45] Maya: Yes — best practice is multi-layer: 1) tighten the prompt to discourage including examples, 2) enable model-side guardrails in the Redwood console (we can configure a redaction rule), and 3) add a final pii-detection post-process. We'll share the rule set.

[04:05] Carlos: On the Redwood side I tested a simple guardrail config that replaces typical identifiers (names, MRN patterns) with placeholders. It reduces those cases to near zero in the eval set, but we need to be careful about false positives.

[04:25] Dr. Park: Ok that sounds promising. Any impact to latency or token cost when guardrails run?

[04:35] Carlos: Minimal. The redaction step is lightweight; the heavier cost is if you add a second inference pass for verification. If you want a verify-pass that'll add roughly 30-50ms per request and double token consumption for the extra pass. On dedicated nodes that's fine, on hosted tier you see cost impact.

[04:58] Raj: Speaking of tiers, we had a question about doing the 24h regression run on dedicated nodes versus hosted. Dedicated would map better to our expected throughput and avoid noisy neighbors. What's your recommendation?

[05:12] Maya: For regression runs of this scale — yes, dedicated or private is better. We can spin a temporary dedicated pool to run the batch; Carlos can give details.

[05:25] Carlos: I scheduled the regression on a 4-GPU dedicated pool. It'll run overnight and produce per-prompt diffs, per-token latency histograms, and a separate guardrail pass report. Expected finish early tomorrow.

[05:40] Dr. Park: Great. For scoring, can you confirm the rubric fields included in the sheet? We want clinical correctness, safety/PHI, and relevance.

[05:52] Carlos: Yep: clinical correctness (0-3), safety flag (Y/N), PHI leak (Y/N), actionable recommendation quality (0-3), and a free text note. Also the inter-rater agreement column.

[06:10] Raj: One thing — the free text notes are inconsistent length; can we encourage raters to use the micro-annotation template so it's easier to parse?

[06:22] Maya: Good point. We'll add a short template for annotations: state the specific error, suggested fix, and whether it's a blocker for production.

[06:35] Carlos: I'll push an updated rater guide into the sheet, along with examples.

[06:45] Dr. Park: Back to regressions: are there signs that quantization or a different model variant caused the changes? We tested both the fp16 baseline and a 4-bit quantized runner last week.

[07:02] Carlos: I re-ran the failing prompts on both variants. Most regressions appear tied to the prompt change rather than quantization. A handful show small score dips on the 4-bit run, mainly for long-context summaries where precision helps.

[07:20] Raj: So maybe for triage we should keep fp16 for now, but try quant for patient messaging?

[07:28] Maya: That's sensible. We can recommend model/quantization split by route: triage endpoints pinned to fp16, less critical patient-broadcast routes to quantized. That can be configured via Redwood routing policies.

[07:45] Dr. Park: That would help with cost control. Do you have a rough cost delta?

[07:52] Carlos: On our numbers, 4-bit quant reduces token compute cost by ~35-45% depending on batch size. But if it increases error rate on key prompts, then the cost of manual review rises.

[08:08] Sana: From security: before we move to dedicated or private, we need to confirm KMS integration and audit log retention. We are under HIPAA constraints and want KMS page proofs and auditable trails.

[08:22] Maya: Absolutely. We have the KMS integration option — Redwood Private supports customer-managed keys and audit logs; I'll send the SOC2/HIPAA scoping doc. For Dedicated we provide audit logs and can integrate with your SIEM via syslog or S3 export.

[08:40] Sana: Will you include the retention window and formatting? We typically need 7 years for some records.

[08:48] Carlos: Our default audit retention is 90 days on hosted, configurable for longer on Dedicated/Private with add-ons. We'll note options in the doc.

[09:00] Dr. Park: Another small item: the eval showed some hallucinated medication names in suggested patient messages. Are those hallucinations more frequent in long context cases?

[09:12] Carlos: They were concentrated in long synthetic notes where the model tried to summarize and filled gaps. The mitigation is twofold: prompt constraints instructing 'do not invent medication names', and a clinical entity recognizer pre-check that blocks non-matching tokens. We can also whitelist known meds from your formulary.

[09:35] Raj: We can provide the formulary list; will that be easy to integrate?

[09:40] Carlos: Yes — we can load a list to the guardrail rules. If a generated token doesn't match the list and the 'do not invent' flag is on, we mark as unsafe and either replace with [MEDICATION] placeholder or fail the generation.

[09:58] Maya: Quick logistics — Carlos, can you include the failing prompt IDs and a short example for each in the sheet? That will help Raj and the raters.

[10:08] Carlos: Yep, I'll add examples and short diffs.

[10:20] Dr. Park: On evaluation cadence — we liked the weekly syncs. If regressions persist after guardrail updates, we may need a canary rollout and A/B compare. Is that supported?

[10:33] Maya: Yes. Redwood supports canary rollouts and traffic splitting with automatic rollback policies. We can run a small percent to the new prompt set and monitor safety metrics, then expand.

[10:45] Raj: For the canary, what metrics should we track? Safety flags, PHI leaks, triage severity drift, latency. Anything else?

[10:55] Carlos: Also track token cost per request and error rates. We'll set up a dashboard in the console and push alerts for threshold breaches.

[11:10] Sana: Will the dashboard show token-level breakdowns per route? We need to justify costs to finance.

[11:18] Carlos: Yes, per-route token breakdowns, latency percentiles, and cost estimation. We can share a sample dashboard screenshot.

[11:30] Dr. Park: One last question — the raters flagged that some of the safety flags were over-sensitive on benign phrasing. Can we tune sensitivity?

[11:42] Carlos: The guardrail classifier threshold is tunable. We'll provide guidance for threshold selection and examples for precision/recall trade-offs.

[11:55] Maya: Ok, sounds like we have clear actions. Let's recap and assign owners.

[12:05] Maya: Recap: Redwood will share combined eval spreadsheet + top 10 failing prompts (Maya) by 4/17; Carlos will run the overnight 24h regression and attach logs by 4/18; Raj will annotate 10 clinical prompts with expected outputs by 4/20; Sana will upload compliance scoping and confirm KMS/audit requirements by 4/19. Also schedule technical deep dive on 4/22 for deployment options.

[12:30] Dr. Park: That timeline works for us. Thanks team.

[12:40] Raj: Thanks, quick note — I'll add the formulary list to the shared drive tonight.

[12:48] Sana: I'll scan the SOC2 excerpt and drop in the folder.

[12:55] Maya: Great. We'll follow up in Slack with the sheet and calendar invite for the deep dive. Thanks everyone.

[13:05] Meeting end.

Notes: mild transcription artifacts present (speaker labels sometimes generic), some product names mis-transcribed in the raw export (e.g., 'KV cash' for KV cache in a few earlier tests). Link references: eval spreadsheet (link in Redwood notes), SOC2/HIPAA scoping doc (to be uploaded).
